# Run agents in parallel

> Compare the ways Claude Code can take on multiple tasks at once: subagents, agent view, agent teams, and dynamic workflows.

[Subagents](/en/sub-agents), [agent view](/en/agent-view), [agent teams](/en/agent-teams), and [dynamic workflows](/en/workflows) each parallelize work in a different way. The right one depends on whether you want to stay in each conversation yourself, hand tasks off and check back later, or have Claude coordinate a group of workers for you.

| Approach                           | What it gives you                                                                                                                                         | Use it when                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| :--------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Subagents](/en/sub-agents)        | Delegated workers inside one session that do a side task in their own context and return a summary                                                        | A side task would flood your main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents you won't reference again                                                                                |
| [Agent view](/en/agent-view)       | One screen to dispatch and monitor sessions running in the background, opened with `claude agents`. Research preview                                      | You have several independent tasks and want to hand them off, check status at a glance, and step in only when one needs you                                                                         |
| [Agent teams](/en/agent-teams)     | Multiple coordinated sessions with a shared task list and inter-agent messaging, managed by a lead. Experimental and disabled by default                  | You want Claude to split a project into pieces, assign them, and keep the workers in sync                                                                                                           |
| [Dynamic workflows](/en/workflows) | A script that runs many subagents and cross-checks their results, for work too big to coordinate one turn at a time or that needs more than a single pass | A job outgrows a handful of subagents, or you want findings verified against each other: a codebase-wide audit, a 500-file migration, cross-checked research, or a plan drafted from several angles |

In every approach the workers are Claude sessions. To involve a different tool, expose it to Claude as an [MCP server](/en/mcp).

Two more tools support this work without being a way to run agents themselves:

* [Worktrees](/en/worktrees) give each session a separate git checkout, so parallel sessions never edit the same files. Use them for sessions you run yourself. Agent view moves each dispatched session into its own worktree automatically, and subagents you spawn can each get one too.
* [`/batch`](/en/commands) is a [skill](/en/skills) that has Claude split one large change into 5 to 30 worktree-isolated subagents that each open a pull request. It's a packaged use of subagents and worktrees, not a separate coordination style.

A few other features run Claude without you driving each step, but they solve a different problem than splitting work across agents:

* A [background bash command](/en/interactive-mode#background-bash-commands) runs one shell command without blocking the conversation. It doesn't spawn an agent.
* A [forked subagent](/en/sub-agents#fork-the-current-conversation) is a subagent that inherits your full conversation context instead of starting fresh. It's a way to spawn a subagent, not a separate surface.
* A [routine](/en/routines) runs a session on a schedule in Anthropic's cloud, not in parallel on your machine.

<Note>
  Running several sessions or subagents at once multiplies token usage. See [Costs](/en/costs) for usage and rate-limit details.
</Note>

## Choose an approach

The right approach depends on who coordinates the work, whether the workers need to communicate, and whether they edit the same files:

* **Who coordinates the work?**
  * Claude delegates and collects results inside one conversation: [subagents](/en/sub-agents)
  * You hand off independent tasks and check back later: [agent view](/en/agent-view)
  * Claude plans, assigns, and supervises a group of workers: [agent teams](/en/agent-teams), experimental and disabled by default
  * A script holds the plan instead of Claude's turn-by-turn judgment: [dynamic workflows](/en/workflows). See [how workflows compare to subagents and skills](/en/workflows#when-to-use-a-workflow)
* **Do the workers need to talk to each other?** Subagents report results back to the conversation that spawned them, and agent view sessions report only to you. Teammates in an agent team share a task list and message each other directly.
* **Do the tasks touch the same files?** Isolate the work with [worktrees](/en/worktrees). Subagents and sessions you run yourself can each use a separate worktree. Agent teams don't isolate teammates in worktrees, so [partition the work](/en/agent-teams#avoid-file-conflicts) so each teammate owns a different set of files.

## Check on running work

The command for checking on running work depends on which approach you used:

* For background sessions, `claude agents` opens [agent view](/en/agent-view): one screen showing every session, its state, and which ones need your input.
* For subagents in the current session, `/agents` opens a panel with a **Running** tab listing live subagents and a **Library** tab where you [create and edit custom subagents](/en/sub-agents#use-the-%2Fagents-command). Despite the similar name, this is separate from `claude agents`.
* For anything running in the background of the current session, `/tasks` lists each item and lets you check on, attach to, or stop it.
* For dynamic workflows, `/workflows` lists running and completed runs, the phase each is in, and how many agents have finished.

For a desktop view of all your sessions, see [parallel sessions in the desktop app](/en/desktop#work-in-parallel-with-sessions).

## Learn more

Each guide below covers setup and configuration for one approach:

* [Create custom subagents](/en/sub-agents): define reusable specialists and control which tools they can use.
* [Manage agents with agent view](/en/agent-view): dispatch sessions, watch their state, and attach when one needs you.
* [Orchestrate agent teams](/en/agent-teams): set up a lead and teammates, assign tasks, and review their work.
* [Orchestrate dynamic workflows](/en/workflows): run a bundled workflow or have Claude write one that runs many subagents and verifies their findings against each other.
* [Run parallel sessions with worktrees](/en/worktrees): start Claude in an isolated checkout, control what gets copied in, and clean up afterward.

# Extend Claude with skills

> Create, manage, and share skills to extend Claude's capabilities in Claude Code. Includes custom commands and bundled skills.

Skills extend what Claude can do. Create a `SKILL.md` file with instructions, and Claude adds it to its toolkit. Claude uses skills when relevant, or you can invoke one directly with `/skill-name`.

Create a skill when you keep pasting the same instructions, checklist, or multi-step procedure into chat, or when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact. Unlike CLAUDE.md content, a skill's body loads only when it's used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it.

<Note>
  For built-in commands like `/help` and `/compact`, and bundled skills like `/debug` and `/code-review`, see the [commands reference](/en/commands).

  **Custom commands have been merged into skills.** A file at `.claude/commands/deploy.md` and a skill at `.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md` both create `/deploy` and work the same way. Your existing `.claude/commands/` files keep working. Skills add optional features: a directory for supporting files, frontmatter to [control whether you or Claude invokes them](#control-who-invokes-a-skill), and the ability for Claude to load them automatically when relevant.
</Note>

Claude Code skills follow the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) open standard, which works across multiple AI tools. Claude Code extends the standard with additional features like [invocation control](#control-who-invokes-a-skill), [subagent execution](#run-skills-in-a-subagent), and [dynamic context injection](#inject-dynamic-context).

# Create custom subagents

> Create and use specialized AI subagents in Claude Code for task-specific workflows and improved context management.

Subagents are specialized AI assistants that handle specific types of tasks. Use one when a side task would flood your main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents you won't reference again: the subagent does that work in its own context and returns only the summary. Define a custom subagent when you keep spawning the same kind of worker with the same instructions.

Each subagent runs in its own context window with a custom system prompt, specific tool access, and independent permissions. When Claude encounters a task that matches a subagent's description, it delegates to that subagent, which works independently and returns results. To see the context savings in practice, the [context window visualization](/en/context-window) walks through a session where a subagent handles research in its own separate window.

<Note>
  Subagents work within a single session. To run many independent sessions in parallel and monitor them from one place, see [background agents](/en/agent-view). For sessions that communicate with each other, see [agent teams](/en/agent-teams).
</Note>

Subagents help you:

* **Preserve context** by keeping exploration and implementation out of your main conversation
* **Enforce constraints** by limiting which tools a subagent can use
* **Reuse configurations** across projects with user-level subagents
* **Specialize behavior** with focused system prompts for specific domains
* **Control costs** by routing tasks to faster, cheaper models like Haiku

Claude uses each subagent's description to decide when to delegate tasks. When you create a subagent, write a clear description so Claude knows when to use it.

# Hook Event Names and Matcher Behavior

## Valid Hook Event Names

The documentation lists these exact hook event names:

**Session-level events:**
- `SessionStart`
- `Setup`
- `SessionEnd`

**Per-turn events:**
- `UserPromptSubmit`
- `UserPromptExpansion`
- `Stop`
- `StopFailure`

**Agentic loop events:**
- `PreToolUse`
- `PostToolUse`
- `PostToolUseFailure`
- `PermissionRequest`
- `PermissionDenied`
- `PostToolBatch`
- `SubagentStart`
- `SubagentStop`
- `TaskCreated`
- `TaskCompleted`

**Async/standalone events:**
- `Notification`
- `MessageDisplay`
- `TeammateIdle`
- `PreCompact`
- `PostCompact`
- `Elicitation`
- `ElicitationResult`
- `ConfigChange`
- `CwdChanged`
- `FileChanged`
- `WorktreeCreate`
- `WorktreeRemove`
- `InstructionsLoaded`

## PreToolUse, SubagentStart, SubagentStop Details

### PreToolUse
- **When it fires:** Before a tool call executes. Can block it.
- **Matcher:** Filters on `tool_name` (e.g., `"Bash"`, `"Edit|Write"`, `"mcp__memory__.*"`)
- **Matchers that match**: Any tool name (exact string, pipe-separated list, or regex)
- **Can block:** Yes (exit code 2 or `permissionDecision: "deny"`)

### SubagentStart
- **When it fires:** When a subagent is spawned
- **Matcher:** Filters on agent type (e.g., `"general-purpose"`, `"Explore"`, `"Plan"`, or custom agent names)
- **Can block:** No
- **Decision control:** No blocking; used for side effects like logging

### SubagentStop
- **When it fires:** When a subagent finishes
- **Matcher:** Filters on agent type (same values as `SubagentStart`)
- **Can block:** Yes
- **Decision control:** Exit code 2 or `{"decision": "block"}` prevents the subagent from stopping

## Matcher Field Behavior

The `matcher` field evaluation depends on its content:

| Matcher Value | Evaluated As | Example |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `"*"`, `""`, or omitted | Match all | Fires on every occurrence |
| Only letters, digits, `_`, `\|` | Exact string or `\|`-separated list | `Bash` or `Edit\|Write` |
| Contains any other character | JavaScript regex | `^Notebook` or `mcp__memory__.*` |

### Key Matching Rules

**For tool events** (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, etc.):
- Matcher filters on `tool_name`
- Example: `"mcp__memory__.*"` matches all Memory server tools
- Can refine further with the `if` field using permission rule syntax

**For non-tool events**, matchers filter on different fields:
- `SessionStart`: how session started (`startup`, `resume`, `clear`, `compact`)
- `SubagentStart`/`SubagentStop`: agent type
- `Notification`: notification type
- `FileChanged`: literal filenames to watch (not regex)

**Omitting the matcher** makes the hook fire on every occurrence of the event.

Based on the search results, here's information about the Claude Code agent file format:

## Agent File Format

Subagents are defined in Markdown files with YAML frontmatter. Project-level agents are stored in `.claude/agents/` inside your project directory.

## YAML Frontmatter Structure

The file itself has two parts: the YAML front matter at the top (between --- delimiters), and the agent's system prompt in the markdown body below.

The YAML frontmatter contains the following key properties:

- name, description, and tools
- The required metadata includes name and description, which are pre-loaded into the system prompt at startup.

## Example Structure

A typical frontmatter looks like: `--- name: code-reviewer description: Reviews code changes for quality, style, and correctness tools: Read, Grep, Glob ---`

The body is the system prompt that defines the subagent's role.

## Agent Locations

Project-level agents (in `.claude/agents/`) are specific to that repo, while user-level agents (in `~/.claude/agents/`) follow you everywhere.

Perfect! Now I have all the information needed. Let me provide you with authoritative, documented answers:

---

## Authoritative Answers on Claude Code Configuration

### 1. **Hook event names** — YES, both exist

`SubagentStart` and `SubagentStop` are **valid, documented hook events**. Your settings.json is using them correctly.

**Complete list of valid agentic loop hook events:**
- `SubagentStart` ✓
- `SubagentStop` ✓
- `PreToolUse`
- `PostToolUse`
- `PostToolUseFailure`
- `PermissionRequest`
- `PermissionDenied`
- `PostToolBatch`
- `TaskCreated`
- `TaskCompleted`

(Plus session-level events like `SessionStart`, `Setup`, `SessionEnd`, and per-turn events like `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, etc.)

**Source:** [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md)

---

### 2. **Firing a hook when subagents spawn** — Your config is CORRECT

Your current hook configuration is the **correct pattern**:

```json
"SubagentStart": [
  {
    "matcher": "harness-",
    "hooks": [
      {
        "type": "command",
        "command": "echo '🔧 HARNESS: subagente iniciando' >&2"
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

**Why this works:**
- `SubagentStart` fires **when a subagent is spawned** (via the `Agent` tool — note: not `Task`, it's `Agent`)
- `matcher: "harness-"` filters on **agent name** (any agent whose name starts with `harness-` will trigger this)
- The command echoes to stderr (`>&2`), so the user sees the message immediately

**Important clarification:** The tool for spawning subagents is called `Agent`, not `Task`. In Claude Code v2.1.63+, `Task` was either renamed or the canonical name is `Agent`. Your settings.json uses `SubagentStart`/`SubagentStop`, which are the correct event names — these fire when the orchestrator delegates to a custom subagent.

**Source:** [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md)

---

### 3. **The matcher field** — Regex, substring, or exact match depending on context

**For SubagentStart/SubagentStop:**
- Matcher filters on **agent name** (the value of `name:` field in the `.claude/agents/*.md` file)
- Your matcher `"harness-"` is treated as a **substring/prefix match** when it contains only alphanumerics, hyphens, and underscores
- To use regex, add any special character: `"harness-.*"` becomes a full regex

**For PreToolUse/PostToolUse:**
- Matcher filters on `tool_name` (e.g., `"Bash"`, `"Edit|Write"`, `"mcp__supabase.*"`)
- Same rule: letters/digits/`_`/`|` = exact/list, anything else = regex

**Source:** [Claude Code Hooks Reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md)

---

### 4. **Agent file frontmatter** — Required vs optional fields

**Your agent files are correctly structured.** Checking your `harness-builder.md`:

```yaml
---
name: harness-builder
description: "..."  # ← quoted to avoid YAML issues
model: sonnet
tools:
  - Read
  - Edit
  - Write
  - Bash
  - Glob
  - Grep
---
```

**Required fields:**
- `name` — **REQUIRED**. Identifier (lowercase, hyphen-separated). Must match filename (e.g., `harness-builder.md` → `name: harness-builder`)
- `description` — **REQUIRED**. This is the routing signal Claude uses to decide when to invoke the agent. Write it to tell Claude *when* this agent should be used.

**Optional fields:**
- `model` — Optional. Valid values are **aliases: `haiku`, `sonnet`, `opus`, `inherit`** OR full pinned IDs like `claude-opus-4-7`. If omitted, inherits session default.
- `tools` — Optional. List of tool names the agent has access to. If omitted, agent has access to all tools (subject to session permissions).

**YAML parsing rule (critical):** If your `description` field contains a **colon-space** (`: `) mid-sentence AND is **unquoted**, YAML will break the parse. Your file correctly **quotes the description**, so you're safe.

```yaml
# ✓ Correct (quoted)
description: "Implementa features, fixes e refactors no MommaERP (Gidape). Usa TDD-first..."

# ❌ Breaks YAML parsing (unquoted colon-space)
description: Implementa features: TDD-first... (would error)
```

**Source:** [Create Custom Subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md) and [MindStudio Guide](https://www.mindstudio.ai/blog/build-custom-sub-agents-claude-code-yaml)

---

### 5. **YAML colon-space bug** — Yes, quoting is the fix

Confirmed: **unquoted YAML with `: ` mid-sentence breaks parsing**. Your current approach of quoting the `description` field is the **correct mitigation**.

```yaml
# If your description needs colons, quote it:
description: "Revisa código para bugs: correctness, style, e performance. Invocado..."
```

---

### 6. **Agent file registration** — Session start ONLY, no hot-reload

**Registration timing:**
- Agent files (`.claude/agents/*.md`) are **read and registered at session start only**
- Edits to agent files **do NOT hot-reload mid-session**
- To pick up changes to an agent file, you must **restart the Claude Code session** (or create a new one)

**File discovery:**
- **Project-level agents:** `.claude/agents/` (inside your repo) — takes precedence
- **User-level agents:** `~/.claude/agents/` (your home directory) — fallback

If the same agent name exists in both locations, the **project-level version wins**.

**Source:** [Create Custom Subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md)

---

## Diagnosis for Silent Agent Failures

Based on the official docs, here's what to check if agents aren't registering:

1. **Session restart:** If you edited an agent file mid-session, agents won't see the changes. Restart Claude Code.
2. **Filename matches name field:** Ensure `harness-builder.md` has `name: harness-builder` (case-sensitive match).
3. **YAML syntax:** Run `cat .claude/agents/harness-builder.md` and visually confirm the YAML frontmatter is clean (no unexpected colons, proper quotes).
4. **Permissions gate:** Even if an agent is registered, the parent session's permissions in `settings.json` still apply. If `Bash(grep:*)` isn't allowed in the session, the agent can't use Grep.
